hook_text: Two soldiers write poems about dying in war. Why do they sound so different?
clip_script: 1914. Rupert Brooke writes that if he dies, some corner of a foreign field will be for ever England. Noble, proud, calm. He has not yet seen the trenches. 1917. Wilfred Owen has. Mud, rats, lice, machine guns and gas. He writes of men bent double like old beggars, and a soldier drowning in gas. The old lie, he calls the idea that dying for your country is sweet. Owen was killed one week before the war ended. Same war. Different experience.
visual_style: A whiteboard split screen: on one side a calm English field and a poem, on the other a muddy trench, barbed wire and a gas cloud.
